files.text:
In the chancel at Stoke d’Abernon, in Surrey, a knight lies in the floor under a sheet of metal as long as he was. He is Sir John d’Aubernoun, in mail from crown to toe, his lance against his shoulder and a lion under his feet biting its shaft, and his was long called the oldest brass in England. Brasses like his were cut from latten, a yellow alloy of copper and zinc beaten into plates in the Low Countries and engraved in London with a burin. The figure was laid in a hollow chiselled to its outline in a slab of Purbeck marble, bedded in pitch and pinned with rivets, and the letters of the epitaph were set round the edge one at a time: Sire Iohan Daubernoun chivaler gist icy, Deu de sa alme eyt mercy. Here lies Sir John d’Aubernoun, knight; God have mercy on his soul.

To take a rubbing you sweep the slab, lay a length of thin white paper over it and tape it down at the corners, then run your fingertips over the paper until you can feel where the metal ends. The heelball is a cake of beeswax, tallow and lampblack that cobblers used to blacken the heels and welts of boots. You rub with its edge, lightly at first and then harder: it rides on the metal and turns the paper black over it, and wherever the burin cut a line the paper sinks a little into the groove and stays white.

The picture comes up the right way round, not mirrored as a print is, because the wax goes on the side of the paper you are looking at. Victorian antiquaries rubbed brasses by the hundred to study armour and dress; by the nineteen-sixties it was a craze, and the brass-rubbing centres sold sticks of gold heelball and rolls of black paper to tourists. So many knees and hands wore so many figures thin that most churches now keep their brasses under carpet and offer a replica instead.

In China the same thing was done a thousand years earlier, and wet. The paper is laid on the stone damp and tamped into every cut with a stiff brush, and when it is nearly dry it is patted with a pad of silk stuffed with cotton and charged with ink, so the face of the stone goes black and the carved strokes of the characters stand out white. It was how the hand of a great calligrapher travelled: the stele stayed in a temple courtyard in Xi’an, but its characters went everywhere in mounted albums, and collectors paid most for the oldest impressions, taken before frost and other rubbings had worn the strokes away. The earliest that survives, of an inscription in the emperor Taizong’s own hand, was found sealed in a cave at Dunhuang.

# brass-rubbing A sheet of thin paper taped over a memorial brass. Rub it and the knight comes up out of blank paper: black where the metal stands, white wherever the burin cut a line, the stone round him a pale grey grain, and every stroke leaving streaks along the way your hand went, the way heelball does. A light pass greys the tops of the paper's fibres; going over it again fills them in. The surface underneath is never shown, only what the wax finds. Enter rubs the whole sheet for you in about six seconds. A second variant lays gold heelball on black paper, as the brass-rubbing centres sold it. ```html ``` The `` is a finished rubbing made by this component. It sizes the sheet and is what you see without JavaScript (and in print). Give it the same proportions as the surface. Or call it yourself: ```js import { brassRubbing } from './brass-rubbing.js'; const sheet = brassRubbing(figure, { wax: 'gold', hint: 'none' }); sheet.rub(); // the automatic rub (instant under reduced motion) sheet.clear(); // a fresh sheet sheet.snapshot(); // data URL of paper + wax (how the no-JS images were made) sheet.state; // { ready, rubbing, anyInk, size } sheet(); // destroy: canvases, listeners, observer ``` ## Options On the element (`data-*`) or in the options object, which wins. | attribute | option | default | | |---|---|---|---| | `data-surface` | `surface` | required | the height map. Grey: white = raised, black = cut, stone in between. Alpha, if present, is the **grip**: how readily the surface takes wax (1 on metal, ~0.3 on worn stone). Same origin | | `data-wax` | `wax` | `black` | `black` heelball on white paper, or `gold` on black paper (gold lays less on the stone) | | `data-hint` | `hint` | `0.5 0.2` | centre of a small patch already rubbed when the sheet arrives, as fractions of the sheet; `none` for blank paper | | `data-reach` | `reach` | `22` | half-width of the rub, css px, for a 460px sheet (it grows with the square root of the sheet's width) | | `data-duration` | `duration` | `6` | seconds for the automatic rub | | `data-tooth` | `tooth` | `assets/paper-tooth.webp` beside the script | the paper's fibre texture (a tileable grey map) | | `data-seed` | `seed` | `3` | creases, tape, streaks and the hint | ## Interaction - **Mouse and pen:** press and drag. Pen pressure counts (light pen, grey rubbing). A quick stroke skims and lays less than a slow one. - **Touch:** the sheet is `touch-action: pan-y`, so the page always scrolls under a vertical swipe. A **sideways** stroke rubs at once. **Hold still for a quarter second** and that touch rubs in any direction until you lift it (the page will not move under it). Real force is used where the screen reports it. - **Keyboard:** the sheet is focusable; **Enter** (or Space) starts the automatic rub: close zigzags working down the sheet, then a lighter diagonal pass, as people actually rub. ## Theming | variable | default | | |---|---|---| | `--br-paper` | `#f4f1e9` (gold: `#1e1b19`) | the paper | | `--br-wax` | `#161413` (gold: `#be964e`) | the heelball | | `--br-sheen` | a warm grey (gold: pale gold) | the burnish on heavily rubbed fibre tops | | `--br-tape` | `#ddcda0` | masking tape | | `--br-shadow` | a hairline and a soft drop | the sheet lying on the stone | | `--accent` | clay | keyboard focus ring | Colours are read once, when the sheet is built. ## How it works 1. **The surface** (made in Python from a line engraving of the brass, see below): the cut lines are grooves (0), the plate is raised (1) with a little wear (the cuts are shallower where the metal is worn), pits and fine scratches; the stone round it is a field of sparse high grains on a low ground. Alpha carries the grip. 2. **Contact.** Built once, at device resolution. The paper is stiff, so it bridges narrow cuts a little: a morphological closing about a pixel wide, blended in at 45%, then a 1-2-1 blur. Hairlines come out a little greyer than broad cuts, as they do in a real rubbing, but close cuts never merge into blobs (a plain blur lowered the metal between them). The heelball is rigid and rides on the local high points: a max filter over about 4 thousandths of the sheet's width, blurred wider than itself so its square corners round off. Contact is `smoothstep(1 - (ride - paper) / 0.4) × grip`, so the wax reaches the paper only where it lies at the top level. Near the plate the crayon rides on the metal and leaves a thin white margin round the figure, exactly as the edge of a brass does. 3. **Creases.** Two to six creases fan in from the taped corners. Along each one the paper stands up a little: the ridge catches wax across the image and the hollows either side skip it. Their light (a bright edge and a soft shade) is drawn above the wax. 4. **Deposit.** Each pointer segment adds wax to a density buffer, per pixel, in proportion to the length of the stroke that passed within reach of it (an exact chord through a disc, so segments chain without seams), times a soft profile across the stroke, times **streaks**: a 1D noise across the stroke direction, in sheet coordinates, so going back and forth over the same place reuses the same streaks, like the lumps on the heelball's edge dragging the same lines. Pressure, speed and a slow wobble scale it. The hand slows at every turn, and the deposit follows its speed relative to its own running average, so each stroke tapers at its turnarounds; it also lands over the first 24 px and its width wanders by ±20%, so the edge of a rubbed patch is soft and ragged rather than straight. 5. **Paper tooth.** The wax goes on the fibres from the top down. Each pixel has a threshold from the fibre map (high fibres low threshold, valleys high), so a light rub is a broken grey grain, more rubbing fills it, and the deepest valleys of the paper stay as white specks even in the blacks. Heavily rubbed fibre tops take a slight burnish. 6. **Render.** Three canvases: the paper (painted once, with the fibre map and a faint cockle), the wax (only the dirty rectangle is recomputed and `putImageData`'d each frame), and an overlay that holds the crease light and the tape, overhanging the sheet. ## Tuning - How dark the stone goes: the grip in the surface's alpha (`GRIP` in the Python: 0.19 on the slab, 0.16 on the floor, rising to about 0.5 in a soft halo round the plate, where the stone was dressed up to the metal and the crayon grazes it). In gold the grip is raised to the power 1.6. - How hard you need to rub: `k` in `deposit()` (0.75) and the threshold curve in `build()` (`0.12 + (1 - tooth)² × 2.6`). - Line softness: the two blur radii on `Hp` (0.7 and 0.5 thousandths of the width) and `depth` (0.4). - Streak character: the octaves in `streak` (periods 1.3 to 42 thousandths) and the exponent 0.95. ## Making a surface Any grey height map works. For these two, the line engravings were cut to the slab, the white region of stone found as the largest connected area around the figure, everything else inside taken as plate, the inked lines inside the plate kept as grooves (slimmed a pixel, since an engraver's cut is finer than the draughtsman's ink) and the outer outline given to the plate's edge. The inscription letters, inked solid in the drawing, become raised brass on stone. A couple of places where the drawing's outline left a gap (the lion's mane) are closed by hand. The draughtsman's ink in the faces is far heavier than a burin's cut and rubbed into a caricature mask, so the 1277 face is redrawn by hand as hairline cuts following Utting's lines (brows into the nose, lids, drilled pupils, nostrils, moustache, mouth), and the 1327 face and both lions' heads are skeletonised to hairlines. The script lives outside the component. ## Cost - Nothing runs while nobody rubs. The rAF loop exists only while a stroke is queued or the automatic rub is going, and the automatic rub pauses off screen. - The sheet is built when it comes within 600px of the screen: about 0.2-0.4 s of work on a laptop for a 440 × 1140 sheet at DPR 2 (two blurs, a max filter, a few full passes over 2 Mpx). Phones take longer, once. - Memory: about 16 bytes per device pixel kept (contact, density, threshold, the wax image), ~32 MB for the desktop demo sheet, ~20 MB on a phone. DPR capped at 2, and the sheet at 4.6 Mpx. - Per frame of rubbing only the stroke's own rectangle is touched. - Assets: two surfaces ~0.7 MB each (they are noise-heavy), the tooth 0.3 MB, and the two no-JS pictures 0.2-0.5 MB, which the browser loads anyway because they size the sheet. ## Accessibility and reduced motion - The figure is `role="img"` with an `aria-label` explaining how to rub it, focusable, with a visible focus ring. Enter rubs; a polite live region says when the rubbing is started and finished. The `` keeps its alt text. - `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce`: the sheet arrives fully rubbed. Rubbing by hand still works on top of it. - Without JavaScript, the finished rubbing is an ordinary image. ## Credits - The two brasses of Sir John d’Aubernoun at Stoke d’Abernon, Surrey, from the wood engravings (signed Utting) in the *Surrey Archaeological Collections*, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons. Details in `assets/credits.json`. - Paper tooth: procedural, made for this component. No third-party code.
